cards.statement: After x=old; (x=new), Bash leaves x equal to new in the enclosing shell.
cards.explanation: A parenthesized group runs in a subshell, leaving the enclosing x equal to old. A brace group executes in the current shell environment.
cards.misconception: A parenthesized assignment changes the enclosing shell's variable.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Compound Commands and Command Execution Environment

cards.statement: With noclobber enabled, Bash keeps that option enabled when it starts a parenthesized subshell.
cards.explanation: A parenthesized subshell starts with a copy of the enclosing shell's options, including the enabled noclobber setting.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Command Execution Environment

cards.statement: Bash treats an opening { attached to the following command name as a brace group delimiter.
cards.explanation: Bash recognizes { as a reserved word when a word boundary separates it from the command list, as in { printf x; }.
cards.misconception: An opening brace separates itself from an adjacent command name.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Compound Commands

cards.statement: Bash accepts a newline before } to terminate a brace group's command list.
cards.explanation: A newline terminates the command list before the closing brace, so a multiline brace group uses that newline in place of a semicolon.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Compound Commands

cards.statement: With an earlier synchronous pipeline stage still running, Bash resumes its script when the final stage ends.
cards.explanation: Bash waits for the participating pipeline commands to terminate before continuing, even when the final command has already finished.
cards.misconception: Bash waits for the final pipeline command while earlier stages finish independently.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Pipelines

cards.statement: With lastpipe on and job control off, Bash retains value=x from printf 'x\n' | while read -r x; do value=$x; done.
cards.explanation: With job control disabled, lastpipe runs this final while loop in the enclosing shell. Its assignment to value persists after the pipeline.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: shopt builtin: lastpipe and Pipelines

cards.statement: Inside a parenthesized group, BASHPID identifies a different process from the one identified by $$.
cards.explanation: $$ keeps the enclosing shell's process ID inside a parenthesized subshell; BASHPID identifies the current Bash process.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: BASHPID and Special Parameters

cards.statement: With job control off and input available on stdin, Bash makes read x & inherit that input stream.
cards.explanation: Bash gives an unredirected asynchronous command /dev/null as stdin when job control is disabled.
cards.misconception: An unredirected background command inherits the script's stdin while job control is disabled.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Command Execution Environment

cards.statement: Bash expands <(printf x) to a filename argument in printf '%s' <(printf x).
cards.explanation: The process substitution inserts a pathname into the command's argument list. The outer printf receives and prints that pathname as text.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Process Substitution

cards.statement: Bash uses the filename from >(cmd) to supply cmd's standard output to the calling command.
cards.explanation: Writes to the filename produced by >(cmd) feed cmd's standard input.
cards.misconception: The >(list) process-substitution form supplies the list's output to its caller.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Process Substitution

cards.statement: Bash executes the list in <(producer) asynchronously with the command using the resulting filename.
cards.explanation: Bash launches the process-substitution list as asynchronous work; completing that list is separate from executing its enclosing command.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Process Substitution

cards.statement: With pipefail enabled, Bash reports a failed command for true < <(exit 7).
cards.explanation: The outer true returns status zero. The process-substitution child exits separately with status 7, so pipefail leaves the outer command successful.
cards.misconception: pipefail folds a process-substitution child's failure into the enclosing command's status.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Process Substitution and Exit Status

cards.statement: With OPTIND=1, getopts 'f:' opt -f config consumes config as the argument for option f.
cards.explanation: A colon after f in optstring marks f as taking an argument. getopts consumes config as that option's argument.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: getopts builtin

cards.statement: With OPTIND=1, getopts 'f:' opt -f config stores f in OPTARG.
cards.explanation: getopts stores the consumed option argument in OPTARG. For -f config, OPTARG contains config.
cards.misconception: OPTARG stores the option letter instead of its argument.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: getopts builtin: OPTARG

cards.statement: With OPTIND=1, getopts 'f:' opt -f value tail leaves OPTIND pointing to value.
cards.explanation: After consuming -f and its argument value, getopts sets OPTIND to 3, the position of the next argument tail.
cards.misconception: OPTIND points to the argument consumed by the current option.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: getopts builtin: OPTIND

cards.statement: With OPTIND=1 and set -- -a, getopts 'ab' opt -b assigns b to opt.
cards.explanation: Supplying arguments after the result variable makes getopts parse that explicit list. Here it parses -b while the shell's positional parameters hold -a.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: getopts builtin

cards.statement: With OPTIND=1, getopts ':f:' opt -f assigns : to opt when the argument is missing.
cards.explanation: A leading colon selects silent error reporting. For a missing option argument, getopts sets the result variable to : and OPTARG to the option letter.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: getopts builtin: Silent error reporting

cards.statement: With OPTIND=3, Bash moves OPTIND to the start when set -- supplies a fresh argument list.
cards.explanation: OPTIND retains parser state within the shell. A script resets OPTIND to 1 before parsing a fresh argument list.
cards.misconception: Replacing positional parameters resets getopts's parser position.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: getopts and set builtins

cards.statement: For input line a\b, read -r value assigns the literal text a\b to value.
cards.explanation: The -r option makes read retain a backslash as input data. The backslash in a\b remains in value.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: read builtin: -r

cards.statement: For line 'one:two::three', IFS=: read first rest assigns 'two::three' to rest.
cards.explanation: When read receives more fields than variable names, it assigns the remaining fields and their intervening delimiters to the last name.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: read builtin: Field assignment

cards.statement: With indexed a=(old), read -a a appends fields from line 'new value' after old.
cards.explanation: read -a removes the array's existing elements before assigning the input fields. Here a contains new and value after read.
cards.misconception: read -a appends to the existing array contents.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: read builtin: -a

cards.statement: Bash treats '|!' as a complete input delimiter string in read -d '|!' value.
cards.explanation: read -d uses the first character of its delimiter argument. Here a | character ends the read.
cards.misconception: read -d matches the entire delimiter argument as a string.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: read builtin: -d

cards.statement: With descriptor 3 supplying ' a b ' plus a newline, read -u 3 stores ' a b ' in REPLY.
cards.explanation: read -u 3 reads from descriptor 3. Supplying no variable names selects REPLY, which retains the line's surrounding spaces after the ending delimiter is removed.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: read builtin: -u and REPLY

cards.statement: With value writable, Bash makes read -r value succeed for unterminated input 'last' followed by EOF.
cards.explanation: read assigns last to value, but encountering EOF before the newline gives read a nonzero status. Data assignment and successful completion are separate outcomes.
cards.misconception: Assigning text from a final unterminated line makes read return success.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: read builtin: End of file
